questions.question_text: What feature does the graph of $y=x^{7}$ have at the origin?

options.why: Treated the odd power $7$ as if it were even, which would give a turning point.
Confused a polynomial power curve with a hyperbola.
Power curves are smooth; a corner is not a feature of $y=x^{n}$.

questions.solution_text:
$y=x^{7}$
$n=7$ is odd, so the graph has a **point of inflection** at the origin.

options.why: An odd power has arms going opposite ways; here both arms rise together.

options.text: Neither — it is a straight line
options.why: The curve bends, so it is not linear ($n=1$).
The symmetric U-shape with both arms up shows the power is even.

questions.solution_text: Both arms rise the same way from a turning point at the origin, with symmetry about the $y$-axis, so $n$ is **even**.

questions.question_text: How does the graph of $y=\frac{1}{4}x^{5}$ compare with the graph of $y=x^{5}$?

options.why: Treated a positive coefficient less than $1$ as if it were greater than $1$.
Treated the multiplying factor as an added constant.
Treated the positive coefficient $\frac{1}{4}$ as negative.

questions.solution_text: Since $0<\frac{1}{4}<1$, the curve $y=\frac{1}{4}x^{5}$ is **wider (flatter)** than $y=x^{5}$, still passing through the origin.

questions.question_text: How does the graph of $y=3x^{3}$ compare with the graph of $y=x^{3}$?

options.why: A coefficient with $|k|>1$ steepens the curve; $|k|<1$ would flatten it.
A coefficient multiplies the curve; it does not translate it vertically.
The coefficient $3$ is positive, so there is no reflection.

questions.solution_text: Since $|3|>1$, the curve $y=3x^{3}$ is **narrower (steeper)** than $y=x^{3}$, still through the origin.

Treated the constant outside the power as a term inside the bracket.
Applied the horizontal-shift rule to the constant outside the power.
Read the positive bracket constant as a shift right instead of left.
Treated the bracket constant as a vertical shift and reversed its sign.

questions.solution_text: $y=4(x-2)^{3}+6$ shifts $y=4x^{3}$ by $2$ units right and $6$ units up.

options.why: Took the direction straight from the $-4$ in $(x-4)$, so the horizontal shift was read as left instead of right.
Applied the opposite-sign rule to the vertical shift as well, so the $+1$ was read as a shift down.
Rewrote the equation as $y-1=(x-4)^{3}$ and read both subtractions as negative directions, giving left and down.

questions.solution_text: $y=(x-4)^{3}+1$ shifts $y=x^{3}$ by $4$ units right and $1$ unit up.

options.why: The inflection point is below the origin, so the shift is $-3$, not $+3$.
The curve is increasing, so $k$ is positive, not negative.
Read $-3$ as a horizontal shift; the inflection is on the $y$-axis, so it is vertical.

questions.solution_text: The point of inflection is at $(0,-3)$ and the curve is increasing. Of the supplied equations, only $y=x^{3}-3$ has both features.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly compares $y=x^{2}$ and $y=x^{6}$ near the origin?

options.text: $y=x^{6}$ is flatter near the origin than $y=x^{2}$
$y=x^{6}$ is steeper near the origin than $y=x^{2}$
options.why: A higher even power flattens near the turning point, not steepens.

options.text: $y=x^{6}$ has a point of inflection at the origin
options.why: An even power has a turning point, not a point of inflection.
The positive coefficient keeps both arms pointing upward.

questions.solution_text:
A higher even power flattens near the turning point but rises more steeply further out.
So near the origin $y=x^{6}$ is **flatter** than $y=x^{2}$.

Reversed the direction of the vertical shift given by $-9$.
Read the bracket constant directly as the horizontal direction and reversed the vertical direction.

questions.solution_text: $y=\frac{1}{2}(x+7)^{6}-9$ shifts $y=\frac{1}{2}x^{6}$ by $7$ units left and $9$ units down.

questions.question_text:
A power curve $y=x^{n}$ passes through the origin, and both of its arms point upward.
Is $n$ odd or even, and what feature is at the origin?

options.text: Odd, with a point of inflection
options.why: Odd powers send the two arms in opposite directions, not both upward.

options.text: Even, with a point of inflection
options.why: Even powers give a turning point, not a point of inflection.
Odd powers give a point of inflection, and their arms do not both point up.

questions.solution_text:
Both arms pointing the same way means equal $\pm x$ give the same $y$, which happens for an **even** power.
An even power curve has a **turning point** at the origin.
